projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Charles Russell Baker was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Today is Saturday, December 27th, 2003 and this is the beginning of an interview with Russell Baker at the home of [address redacted]. Russell Baker is 77 years old, being bom on April 27, 1926. My name is Holly Baker, and I'll be the interviewer. Russell Baker is my Grandfather. He is my father's father. Grandfather, could state for the recording, what war you were in and what you served in?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I was in the U.S. Navy from June 1944 until September 1946 in the U.S. Navy. I was mostly in the Navy Cadets.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I enlisted when I was 17 years old and was programmed into the Navy Air Corps whereby students could be tested or enlist in the Naval Air Corp. Two weeks after I graduated from high school I was in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I was in Albion, Michigan.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Why did you decide to join in the War?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, I thought it was my duty as a male citizen of the United States to serve in the Armed Forces in a world against the axis of powers. There wasn't any question in my mind that it was my duty to do it.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Why did you decide to enlist in the Air Force?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I was interested in flying and interested in airplanes and thought the Navy Air Force was the best place for me.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: How did you feel about the war?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I felt it was something you had to do and we had to defeat the axis of powers in order to safeguard our country in the world as a matter of fact.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Do you recall some of your first days in the service? What were they like? What was training like?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I was inducted into the Navy and had to report to the Naval B-12 Unit at Albion College in Albion, Michigan. From there we went on to basic training and every air force cadet was required to have a year of college. So I started out with my year at Alma College.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you have uniforms?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What did they look like?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: They were the regular Navy seaman's uniform.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What did it feel like to be a part of the Navy training Air Force?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I was very proud to be in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Uh, the first instructor was a Chief Petty Officer named Steve Birkhart. He was the athletic specialist actually. He served as the Chief Petty Officer of the training.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Were you married at the time?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you ever have any thoughts that our side was weaker than the axis of powers?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, we were just at the point of what I entered the service of turning around and becoming superior. The Allies were becoming superior of course, and we would probably win but it would take a great deal of time.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you have any corresponding letters to family and friends?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes, I'd write to my parents at least once a week and they would write me. We were close enough and after the first six weeks I could take a weekend off and come home.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Where did you go during WWII and what camps were you stationed at?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I was stationed at Alma in Chicago, and pre-flight school in Iowa City, Iowa and Otomwa Naval Air Station in Otomwa, Iowa. And three of the four main bases of Corpus Christi Naval Air Force Station.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Do you remember arriving and what were your first thoughts as you arrived?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Glenview was the first large naval air station and I was very impressed with all the activities and so forth and our efforts at the Naval station.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I was 18.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Was that at the age most men enlisted at?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I think the requirement was 18.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What was your jobs or assignments?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: My first assignment was to get a college education.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Where did you go to college?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: At Alma College.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What was one of your most memorable experiences?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, I guess my year at Alma was kind of a routine military and college exposure. Alma College was actually taken over by the Navy. There was probably about 300 of us in the Navy and civilians were probably most of them. The whole life was military at Alma College. The basic classes of instruction were science, mathematics and naval organization and naval history.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What did you study?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: All of those.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Any class that you liked the best?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or awards at college or in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: About how many people were with you in your unit or did you have a unit?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, at Alma there was one single unit. There were roughly 300 or 400 seamen there. At Glenview Naval Air Station we were in units awaiting assignment to pre-flight school so we were in smaller units which did ground crew service.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What was training like? What were some of the chores you had to do every day? GRANFATHER BAKER: We had to make service the planes and make sure they were ready to fly for the next day. Refuel them and inspect them and secure them at the end of the day.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: How many hours did this take a day?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: About 8 to 10.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you fly every day?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No, not every day.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What were the names of the planes?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Most of the planes we service were FMs- GM built or TBMs and torpedo bombers.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What were some of the places that you would fly to?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: We didn't fly every plane.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Any other camps that you got to fly?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: After pre-flight school at Corpus Christi we flew every day.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you go overseas or did you stay around the Naval Air Camp?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No, just stayed at the camp.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you stay in touch with your family by letters or did you go home?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I got to go home once when I was at Corpus Christi.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What was the purpose of the mission when you were at Corpus Christi? Did you test them out?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: The purpose was to learn all the ins and outs of flying, aerial acrobats, landings under duress conditions, simulated landings on aircraft carriers. All those things are required of a naval pilot.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Were some of these things dangerous? Like the acrobats?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes, some of the acrobats were very dangerous and we had to practice them. We had to practice stalling an airplane and bringing them out of a stall which can be quite dangerous. All the aerial acrobatics, if you make a mistake, like during the stall, you'd better have the altitude to bring it out.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Were the planes one-seater or two?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: They were 2.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you carry anything on the planes?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: At Corpus Christi or at your training camp, what was the food like?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I really don't remember, but I don't remember complaining a bit about the food.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies or what were you allowed to bring from home?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Very little from home. Just a few personal belongings- razors. All the rest of it was GI issued.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you every get really stressed out or pressured?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Oh yes, yeah. Building up to the time of day you soloed there was lots of pressure.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What did you guys do in your free time? Did you play cards?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, we played basketball, we played baseball, we were able to do a little fishing in the gulf. That was the main things people did. Sometimes when we had time off, we could leave the base and go into Corpus Christi or we would go up to the ......Pass and try the shrimp. And the shrimp dinner.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What did the camp look like scenery-wise?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, Corpus Christi Naval Air Station was a very, very large compound and it had three outlying navy airfields. From those main airfields, there were smaller air fields so that we covered thousands of acres. The airfields were probably in the neighborhood of 70 airfields. We were assigned an airfield to practice flying and practice landing and an area to practice our aerial maneuvers. It was a very, very large airfield. Probably in the neighborhood of 30 thousand men in uniform.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What was the college like that you attended?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Alma?

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: It was a typical small college that had been converted into a V5/V12 training college. The then Secretary of the Navy, Frank Knox, was a graduate of Alma College and therefore he picked Alma College as one of the Navy VI2 or V5 units. They imported quite a few of the professors because of changing the curriculum. For example, the professor of physics, was Dr. Brown and he was the head of the Physics Department at the University of Berlin prior to the war. He was a highly noted educator. He could read and write seven different languages, including Egyptian Sanscrit. In his physics classes he had memorized the logarithms so that he never had to look in the math book to look up the logarithms. They were all in his head. But he had no other life but education. A very strange person.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: How did people entertain themselves at college or at Corpus Christi?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Why, I think we had a lot of fellowship and we did a lot of things together. Sit down and tell things that they had accomplished, helped each other in our endeavors. We were all assigned roommates. I had two other roommates. All they had was room enough for three desks and three bunks in the room, but the guys would come around and we helped each other in our education desires, in the training. We had a close fellowship because we were all trying to accomplish the same goal.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did they ever bring in entertainers or comedians?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes, at times we had entertainers that would come in and put on shows for us.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What did you do when you went on leave or time off to go away from the camp?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, like I said most of the time we went to the ranches when we were at Corpus Christi, we went to Mexico, Matamoros, San Antonio. But at that time you could go almost anyplace as a uniformed person. You could hitch hike and get free rides or all those kinds of things. I remember when the World Series was going on between the Detroit Tigers and the Chicago Cubs and we walked down to see if we could get in the game and they told us yes, as long as we were willing to sit in the aisle way of the steps to see the ballgame for nothing. So we did that and saw who won the World Series game, but we were always accepted at that time in uniform.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: You said you went to Mexico?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes, to Matamoros a couple of times. I wasn't very impressed.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: You got to go home one time to visit your family?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes, from Corpus Christi. I went home several times from Glenview Naval Air Station. At Iowa, I never did get to go home until pre-flight school was over. My parents did come out to Iowa City one time to see me.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Where in Michigan did they live?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: They lived in Albion.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Do you recall any humorous or unusual things that would go on at camp?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yeah. One humorous thing we did at Corpus Christi down there where the environment is very humid. We had a terrible problem in the barracks with cockroaches. We got together and devised a gag with a pump oil can. And we got aviation fuel and put in the pump oil can and we put a cigarette lighter to make a flame thrower out of it. The guys would chase the cockroaches down the hallways with the flame thrower. But we did get rid of the cockroaches, though.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Our school needs one! Did you guys pull pranks?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Oh, once in a while I suppose we did. I guess one of the biggest pranks we ever pulled that everybody got on trouble for it, but nobody was accused of anything though. We found out that an SMJ which was the North American naval trainer that if you turn the ignition off while you were flying and turned the engine off and turned it right back on, it would backfire. So we would fly over the cattle ranches of Kings Ranch and if you fly moderately close to the cattle as they were rounding them up and let the engine backfire, it would scare the cattle. The ranchers began to complain to the main base Admiral in charge at Corpus Christi and we all got directed not to do that ever again. But that was quite fun to make the cattle scatter.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What were the weather conditions like in Corpus Christi?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: We had all kinds of weather. It was hot and humid. Most of the time we had to prepare for hurricanes. At times storms would come up quickly sometimes, and I can remember coming in one time a storm had come up during the basic training and as the planes came in the men would have to jump on the wings to hold the plane down. The winds were stronger than the landing speed of the aircraft. You could land it but you couldn't hold it down.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you ever practice flying in bad conditions?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No. One thing we were always taught is not to fly through thunderstorms. Go around it. Don't fly in bad conditions. At all costs, avoid them.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What did you think of your officers or the people in charge of you?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, most of our flight instructors were experienced fliers and many of them had seen combat. They would lead the combat and come back as instructors. Some had fought and some of them hadn't. The Naval officers and Marine officers were very competent and very helpful and had been most educated because they had been cadets at one time.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: You said some were brought back from combat? Were they injured?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: They were relieved of duty and they had flown a number of missions and could come back.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What kind of planes did the axis of power fly? Did they fly the same planes as the US had?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes, they flew the same- F4s , German F4s and Corsairs and torpedo bombers. Some of them were even flying boats.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did they have something painted on your planes or their planes to distinguish sides?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Our insignia- the round star.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you keep a journal or anything while you were there?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No. I did keep a flying hours log. I had to keep that.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Was it required?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I do recall that period. We were told that if we wanted to continue we had to sign up for four more years which would involve two years at Annapolis and two years of active duty. Most of us decided that after two and half years in the service on that was enough and we didn't want to spend four more years. We decided to get out. Within a couple of weeks we had to sign up or get out. We were allowed transportation home.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: How far along was the war when you left?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: The war was over at that time. Both in the Pacific and overseas. That's why the Navy made the decision that they didn't train any more aviators unless they wanted to stay in the Navy and get more navy military training in hopes that those who wanted to stay would make a career out of it. I definitely didn't want to make a career out of it.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Who told you that the war was over?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Everyone knew that the war was over. We celebrated VJ Day.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: After you left, where did you go the days afterward?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, I went home and I applied and was accepted to the General Motors Institute but not until the following fall. And therefore I worked at a foundry, Albion Malleable, in the office as an all-around messenger until I could go to school.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I was 21 then

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes, I did and they carried on for quite a few years. After I got out everyone got married. One of my close friends was Dick Carl who when I went on to pre-flight school, he went on to ROTC at University of Michigan. He married a gal that was there in college and she was from Battle Creek, Michigan only 18 miles from Albion. And so we tried to keep track of one another and quite often we would get together when he would come home to see the in-laws. At that time I was out of school, graduated, and engineering graduate and he was out of school as a CPA. We would meet them and have dinner together in Battle Creek. He went on to Cleveland at Cleveland National Bank and I was at that time in Tiffin, Ohio, which wasn't too far from Cleveland. We met several times there. As the years went by we saw each other fewer and fewer times. We were quite close for some time. Some of the other fellows that I corresponded with lasted for about five or six years. One of them was close by Albion and I corresponded with him. I would see him quite often. Some of the other ones I did lose track of. Harry Anderson who was from Manistee, Michigan, whose grandparents founded the Morton Salt Company. I would talk to Harry once in a while. But I haven't seen him for years. My other roommate was Bob Vlasic. You've heard of Vlasic pickles. That was Bob's family. I corresponded with him for a while. But as time went by I lost track of him. I tried him a couple of times. I had a good friend who was Dick Adams who was a Mormon. I tried to find him once. He was from north of Salt Lake City. And I hadn't been able to find him in 15 years. I tried on the Internet, but I still couldn't find him. There were a lot of nice guys. And we had a lot of fun together. It's something I wouldn't have missed for the world but I wouldn't want to have to do it again.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did you know anyone over in Europe?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Then they were all in your base?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Do you belong to any veterans organizations? mD

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: The American Legion.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: What did you do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, I went to school at General Motors Institute and got a degree in engineering and then I went to work for several foundries of General Motors in Saginaw. I worked there for two and a half years and then I got an offer at Albion Malleable to be product engineer there and I accepted that.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Do you attend any reunions still?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: No, I don't. I don't think we've had any reunions of that group. The organization changed so fast. It wasn't a fixed organization like the Third Division or the USS Arizona. I tried to keep track through the American Legion.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did the service- how did the service affect your life?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, I think I realized that from that military life that it is tough on a person, on the family. I have a great deal of respect for the military. They have a lot of snafus but the rules and regulations are reasonable and have reasons for it. If I had my way, I think the country would be better off if every man would have to serve a year in the military after they get out of school because to learn the hardships is the tough part of life in the military. You earn a respect for property and other people's feelings. I think a year in the military would be a good education.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Was your mother or father part of Red Cross or did they help out?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Well, my father was very active in his job as a service representative for Albion Malleable and their sole product was a 100% military product and he serviced companies that made the Army 6x6 and the tanks and he was very much aware of the military and all the kinds of war. My mother helped out, yes, with the Red cw Cross. I guess I never realized until I had a son, that, how much my mother was worried about me while I was gone. I didn't think she should worry about me at the time but I now recognize and realize that she was very worried as long as I was in the service if something happened.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Did the, like, how was life, like, living in a community such as in Michigan? How did life change for them? Were there like food shortages or anything?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: Oh sure. The war changed... there were just things we didn't have. It was tough to get shoes, it was tough to get ... gasoline was rationed, sugar was rationed, and all those kinds of things were rationed. Basically nobody complained. There were some people who tried to work the system, but very few. They all knew they had to make a sacrifice and it was important to make a sacrifice because there was a distinct danger of our way of life here being destroyed. As a service person in uniform wherever you went you were welcomed and people recognized that you were willing to make the sacrifice to help the men in uniform to get the job done.

sp.speaker: Holly Baker
sp.p: Is there anything else that you want to add to the interview?

sp.speaker: Charles Russell Baker
sp.p: I don't think so.
